opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the outcome has been pretty clear, and it's been clear for a long time, though people keep having to relearn it. That's what I tried to say in "The Bitter Lesson." If you look back over seventy years of AI research, the methods that win out in the long run are the general ones, the ones that scale with computation, and that basically means search and learning. The methods where we try to build in what we think we know about how we think lose out eventually.

It happened in chess. People tried to encode human understanding of the game, and then deep search on special hardware beat the world champion. A lot of the chess researchers weren't happy about it; they said it was "just brute force." Then it happened in Go, even more dramatically, with learning from self-play. It happened in speech recognition, where the statistical methods beat the ones built on knowledge of phonemes and the vocal tract. It happened in computer vision with convolutional networks and learned features instead of hand-designed edge detectors and so on.

The reason it's bitter is that building in human knowledge feels good. It's satisfying for the researcher, and it often helps in the short term. You get a nice bump. But it plateaus, and it even gets in the way, because it ties the system to how we think we think, which turns out to be not very accurate. Meanwhile Moore's law, or its generalization, keeps going, and the methods that can use more computation keep improving and eventually overtake you.

So the lesson is that we should build in the meta-methods, the ability to discover, rather than the discoveries themselves. The world is irreducibly complex. We shouldn't try to put simple models of space, objects, agents, and so on into our systems. We should build systems that can find and capture that complexity on their own.

Now, I'll say something that maybe people don't expect from me. Many people take today's large language models as the ultimate vindication of the Bitter Lesson, and in one sense they are: massive computation, general methods. But in another sense they're the opposite, because they're built mostly on imitating human-generated text. They're absorbing human knowledge in enormous quantities. I suspect that eventually they'll hit the same kind of limits, and the systems that win will be the ones that learn from experience, from actually interacting with the world and getting feedback, the way animals do and the way reinforcement learning is meant to. That's the truly scalable source of data. So I'd say the competition has been won by general methods again and again, but we're not done learning the lesson.

r001.rationale: The candidate says general methods that scale with computation—search and learning—have repeatedly won in the long run, while approaches built around human knowledge eventually lose.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the outcome is pretty clear by now, and it's the same outcome we've seen over and over for seventy years. The methods that scale with computation win. That's the whole story of what I called the bitter lesson. In chess, in Go, in speech recognition, in computer vision, and now in language, the researchers who tried to build in their understanding of how the problem works got short-term gains and were then overtaken by people who just let search and learning do the work, with more compute.

And it's bitter because it's a lesson about us. We think we know how our own minds work, and we want to put that in. It feels like the right thing to do. It feels like real science. But what we actually know about how we think is very shallow, and the compute keeps getting cheaper, and so the thing that scales eventually overwhelms the thing that doesn't.

Now, I'd add a caveat that people sometimes miss when they quote me. Large language models are often held up as the triumph of scaling, and in a sense they are. But they're also, in a sense, the biggest knowledge-imbued systems ever built. They're trained to imitate what people wrote. That's human knowledge, just acquired by learning rather than hand-coded. So I'd say the competition isn't really over. The next stage is between systems that learn from people and systems that learn from their own experience, from actually interacting with the world and finding out what happens. I think experience is the real scalable thing. The data from text is finite. The data from living is not.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the outcome is clear: methods that scale with computation win, and approaches that build in human understanding were overtaken by search and learning.

astra-6.text:
I think the lesson of AI’s history is that the general methods win in the long run. People bring their knowledge of a problem to bear, and that often produces an improvement right away. But eventually an approach that makes better use of computation, through search or learning, overtakes it.

That’s what I call the bitter lesson. It’s bitter because we want our understanding to be the thing that makes the system work. We want to tell it what matters, how to represent the world, how to reason about it. And those ideas can be useful, but they tend to reach a ceiling. Search and learning can continue to improve as more computation becomes available.

So I don’t think the lesson is that human ingenuity has no role. It’s that we should put our ingenuity into methods that can discover things, rather than putting what we’ve already discovered into the system. We want agents that can acquire knowledge from their own experience, including knowledge that we don’t have.

r001.rationale: The response says general methods based on search or learning “win in the long run” and eventually overtake approaches built on human-supplied knowledge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the historical lesson is that the general methods win in the long run. We repeatedly find ways to put our knowledge into a system, and that gives us an immediate improvement. It’s very tempting, because we understand the knowledge we’re putting in, and we can see why it ought to help.

But then computation increases, and methods that can take advantage of that computation—particularly search and learning—eventually surpass the systems built around our knowledge. That’s the bitter lesson. It’s bitter because the work of encoding our understanding often turns out to be less important than we thought.

That doesn’t mean there’s no role for human ingenuity. We need ingenuity to discover methods that scale. But we should be trying to build agents that can discover how to solve problems for themselves, rather than building our solutions into them. The things we know are not the limit of what can be known.

r001.rationale: The response says general methods such as search and learning win in the long run and eventually surpass systems built around human knowledge.
